questions.q: Which of the following is the FDA arrangement that Breakthrough Therapy Designation refers to for a drug with breakthrough therapeutic potential?
options: The complete non-clinical test package a company must work through before filing an IND with the regulator.
intellectual property, i.e. IP.
The accelerated pathway the FDA gives to a drug with breakthrough therapeutic potential.
Finding, at the very start of drug development, the molecule the disease genuinely depends on.
questions.why: Breakthrough Therapy Designation is one of the FDA's expedited pathways: it lets developers communicate more frequently with the review division and push the approval forward on earlier clinical data, so that drugs with a major breakthrough reach the market sooner. It changes only the procedural treatment on the regulatory side, not the science itself. The other distractors are the complete non-clinical test package, intellectual property, and the first step of the pipeline — finding the molecule the disease depends on — and none of these is an FDA expedited pathway.

questions.q: Of the two questions asked when selecting a target, what does 'Disease relevance' ask?
options: Whether this molecule matters to the disease itself.
The decision the company makes about which molecule to go after.
The study of how a compound affects a whole animal.
The patient cohort in Phase 1B used to look at side effects and early efficacy.
questions.why: Disease relevance is the first of the two target-selection questions: is this molecule genuinely elevated in patient samples? A molecule can be important to the disease and at the same time completely impossible to turn into a drug; it can also be very easy to make into a drug while being unrelated to the disease. The lecturer uses cytoskeleton as a contrast: it is essential to metastasis, yet it is too important and present everywhere, so it cannot be attacked selectively.

questions.q: What does the first stage of a clinical trial, Phase 1A 'Dose escalation', do?
options: The patient cohort in Phase 1B used to look at side effects and early efficacy.
The whole body of development work carried out before formal human trials.
The stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound.
The first stage of the trial, escalating the dose step by step to find the safety ceiling.
questions.why: Phase 1A is called dose escalation: a small group of patients is given a low dose, toxicity and pharmacokinetics are observed, and the dose is then increased according to pre-set rules until dose-limiting toxicity appears, after which the dose is stepped back to find the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). It produces two outputs: a safety boundary, and the dose range that Phase 2/3 will use; it is Phase 1B that enrols more patients on doses near the MTD.

questions.q: Which question about a target does 'Druggability' ask?
options: Finding, at the very start of drug development, the molecule the disease genuinely depends on.
Whether this molecule can be made into a drug that hits only it and spares everything else.
The stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound.
The study of how a compound affects a whole animal.
questions.why: Druggability is the second of the two target-selection questions: can you find a small molecule that fits into its pocket, an antibody that recognises it, or a stretch of nucleic acid that can target it? K-Ras used to be called undruggable and later no longer was; he uses this example to show that previously undruggable targets are becoming druggable. So 'important' and 'druggable' are two questions that have to be answered separately.

questions.q: In the assessment of a clinical trial, what does 'efficacy' refer to?
options: The FDA's priority review entitlement for applications with major therapeutic breakthroughs.
The study of how a compound affects a whole animal.
The measure of whether a drug really works in the right patients.
The patient cohort in Phase 1B used to look at side effects and early efficacy.
questions.why: efficacy asks whether, in the patient population for whom the drug is intended, the drug actually changes the outcome. It is a different judgement from safety: Phase 1A and 1B deal mainly with safety and dosing, while Phase 2 and Phase 3 are where efficacy is formally measured, and Phase 3 is a large randomised trial comparing the new drug with the current standard of care. Safety decides whether the drug can be used, efficacy decides whether it is worth using.

questions.q: After Phase 1A has escalated the dose to find the maximum tolerated dose, Phase 1B switches to a fixed dose and enrols more patients; this patient cohort, used to look at side effects and early efficacy, is called ______.
options: Expansion cohorts
Dose escalation
preclinical
Priority Review
questions.why: The expansion cohorts of Phase 1B fix the dose established in Phase 1A and enrol more patients, with the aim of seeing the side effects clearly while starting to watch for anyone responding; it is in effect the stage that brings 'safety' and 'preliminary efficacy' in together. Phase 1B involves more patients than 1A and longer follow-up, and true efficacy is only formally measured in Phase 2 and Phase 3.

questions.q: Under the former US patent system, what is the English term for the filing principle that grants priority to whoever actually makes the invention first, rather than to whoever files first?
options: Non-obviousness
patent pool
Freedom to Operate (FTO)
first-to-invent
questions.why: first-to-invent is the filing principle of the former US patent system, which goes to whoever actually made the invention first. On his CRISPR patent timeline, Broad obtained the first CRISPR-Cas9 patent on 15 April 2015 (covering plant and animal cells) under the first-to-invent principle rather than first-to-file, and this principle was gradually replaced by first-to-file in the United States after 2011.

questions.q: In drug development, what does 'Freedom to Operate (FTO)' refer to?
options: intellectual property, i.e. IP.
The patent risk check carried out before commercialisation.
The complete non-clinical test package a company must work through before filing an IND with the regulator.
The stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound.
questions.why: FTO answers a very practical question: if I build this product, will I be sued? It is a separate matter from whether I will obtain a patent — a company that did not invent the tool may be barred from a particular application by someone else's patent. The lecturer uses the two CRISPR patent lines to show that the law can distinguish the invention from the specific application, but that disputes arise where the distinction cannot be drawn cleanly.

questions.q: In animal models, what is put into the mouse in a 'humanised mouse'?
options: The decision the company makes about which molecule to go after.
The FDA's priority review entitlement for applications with major therapeutic breakthroughs.
An animal model that puts human genes into a mouse.
The study of how a compound affects a whole animal.
questions.why: A humanised mouse carries a human disease gene transplanted into a mouse, so that the effect of the gene can be observed in a living organism, which is far quicker and far cheaper than cell culture. But it is still not a human: the metabolism, the dose and the side effects of a drug in a mouse may differ from those in humans, so it is the starting point of the modelling exercise rather than the end point.

questions.q: What does 'IND (Investigational New Drug)' refer to?
options: The application a company must submit before being permitted to test a drug in humans.
The informal meeting held with the FDA before the company formally submits the IND.
The early consultation that comes before the pre-IND meeting.
The stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound.
questions.why: The IND is an application made to the regulator (the FDA in the United States), covering CMC (chemistry, manufacturing and quality control) data, non-clinical study reports (safety, pharmacokinetics, toxicology), and the clinical plan with arrangements for subject protection. An effective IND means the drug is permitted to enter human trials, and the sequence is pre-IND meeting → non-clinical research and IND-enabling studies → Phase 1A → Phase 1B → Phase 2/3.

questions.q: According to the lecturer's description of the process, what must a company complete before submitting an IND application?
options: The application a company must submit before being permitted to test a drug in humans.
The stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound.
The informal meeting held with the FDA before the company formally submits the IND.
The complete non-clinical test package a company must work through before filing an IND with the regulator.
questions.why: IND-enabling studies are the complete non-clinical test package that a company works through before filing an IND with the regulator, and they have two main parts: pharmacology and toxicology, covering whether the compound does what is expected in cells and what it does to a whole animal; and quality data such as CMC. Only once this package is finished is the company in a position to file an IND, because it turns 'we believe this drug is effective and safe' into an evidence chain that the regulator can check item by item.

questions.q: On the practical level of drug development, what is 'IP'?
options: The filing principle of the former US patent system.
intellectual property, i.e. IP.
The 'non-obviousness' requirement that a patent application must pass.
A licensing alliance in which several patent holders license one another.
questions.why: IP, short for intellectual property, is a whole body of legal questions: who has the right to use a given technology. In the CRISPR example it becomes a real commercial conflict, with two patent lines each advancing their own claims, and there is a grey area where the law can separate the invention itself from a specific application but cannot do so cleanly. For scientists who want to do business, IP is a practical consideration when choosing a project, just as druggability is.

questions.q: In the stretch of work after target identification and before preclinical work, what does 'medicinal chemistry' refer to?
options: Finding, at the very start of drug development, the molecule the disease genuinely depends on.
The study of how a compound affects a whole animal.
The stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound.
The patient cohort in Phase 1B used to look at side effects and early efficacy.
questions.why: Medicinal chemistry is the stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound: a biologically meaningful target must still be made into a molecule with the right shape, solubility and potency before it can become a drug. It belongs to the pharmaceutical company's process and is usually not part of a biologist's research; this stage has the highest failure rate, so the company runs many chemistry series at the same time, and only a few molecules are pushed on to the animal study stage.

questions.q: In preclinical research, what is the English term for the mechanism of action used to show that a compound really acts on the intended target site?
options: MOA
Druggability
Expansion cohorts
pre-IND
questions.why: MOA stands for mechanism of action — the evidence of what the compound actually does. Together with toxicology it forms the two cornerstones of the preclinical stage: the former shows that the drug really acts on the intended site in cells and animals, the latter shows what side effects it has in a whole animal. MOA has to be established first because the same compound may act in different ways; without knowing how it works, the dose design that follows would be guesswork.

questions.q: What is the English term for the 'non-obviousness' requirement that a patent application must pass, which demands that the invention is not merely a straightforward extension of known technology?
options: first-to-invent
patent pool
Freedom to Operate (FTO)
Non-obviousness
questions.why: Non-obviousness is the 'non-obviousness' requirement that every patent application must pass: an invention cannot simply be a straightforward extension of known technology, since anyone could then make it, so it must contribute something non-obvious. The lecturer uses the CRISPR patent war to show that what was disputed was precisely whether the application was an obvious extension of existing knowledge, and whether the invention itself can be separated from a specific application.

questions.q: What is the English term for an alliance in which several patent holders put their patents into the same pool, license one another on agreed terms, and each go on to develop their own applications?
options: Freedom to Operate (FTO)
patent pool
Non-obviousness
first-to-invent
questions.why: A patent pool is a licensing alliance in which patent holders license one another. When neither of the two CRISPR patent lines could monopolise the field on its own, one solution was to establish a patent pool: everyone puts their patents into the same pool, licenses one another on agreed terms, and each is then free to develop its own applications — Broad has been pushing in this direction. This is the most practical lesson intellectual property teaches in biotechnology: being able to make something and being able to sell it legally are two different questions.

questions.q: Before formally submitting the IND, a company holds an informal meeting with the FDA to go through the protocol in detail, and usually leaves with a written agreement; what is the English name of this meeting?
options: pre-pre-IND
IND-enabling studies
pre-IND
preclinical
questions.why: The pre-IND is the informal meeting held with the FDA before the company formally submits the IND. Its purpose is not to obtain the regulator's endorsement but to lay the plan out and discuss it: which animal model to choose, which data need to be assembled first, what the regulator's expectations are. At the end of the meeting the company usually has a written agreement in hand, and the experiments that follow are designed against that document.

questions.q: At the first contact with the regulator, when a company brings only its roughest ideas to ask whether a target is worth pursuing and which model to use for assessment, what is the English term for that early consultation?
options: pre-pre-IND
pre-IND
preclinical
IND (Investigational New Drug)
questions.why: The pre-pre-IND is an early consultation that comes before the pre-IND meeting. At first contact the company usually brings only its roughest ideas: is this target worth pursuing, which model should be used to assess it, which experiments should be prepared first; once the direction is settled the pre-IND meeting is held to go through the protocol in detail. Both are preparatory steps before the formal IND, and at this stage the company is usually not asking about data but about whether the regulator is willing to hear the story of the same direction.

questions.q: The body of development work carried out before formal human trials is called ______; it comprises MOA, toxicology and the quality data for the drug itself, and the three together make up the content of IND-enabling studies.
options: medicinal chemistry
Expansion cohorts
Breakthrough Therapy Designation
preclinical
questions.why: Preclinical is the whole body of development work carried out before formal human trials, and it has two parts: MOA, showing that the compound really acts on the intended site, and toxicology, showing what it does to a whole animal; in addition there is the quality data for the drug itself, and the three together make up the content of IND-enabling studies. If the conclusions at this step are not encouraging, the IND will not be filed; safety data is far more often the true end point than efficacy data.

questions.q: Of the three FDA mechanisms the lecturer named alongside Breakthrough Therapy Designation and Orphan Drug Designation, the one that grants priority in the review timeline is ______.
options: patent pool
Priority Review
pre-IND
Druggability
questions.why: Priority Review is the FDA's priority review entitlement for applications with major therapeutic breakthroughs; like Breakthrough Therapy Designation and Orphan Drug Designation, it is one of the three FDA mechanisms the lecturer named on his slides. The difference is that Breakthrough Therapy is for a drug with breakthrough potential, whereas Priority Review gives priority in the review timeline, and Orphan Drug gives seven years of market exclusivity for rare diseases. The three differ only in the procedural treatment they receive on the regulatory side and do not affect the science itself.

questions.q: To make a drug you need a way of getting at the target: a pocket a small molecule can fit into, a surface an antibody can bind, or a sequence a stretch of nucleic acid can pair with. What is this property of being attackable structurally called ______.
options: Disease relevance
Target nomination
structural tractability
first-to-invent
questions.why: Structural tractability is whether the molecule can be attacked structurally — that is, whether there is a way of getting at it: a pocket a small molecule can fit into, a surface an antibody can bind, or a sequence a stretch of nucleic acid can pair with. This is a different question from how important it is in the disease: many important molecules are too important and present everywhere, so there is no way to attack them alone.

questions.q: The first step of the whole drug development pipeline, finding the molecule the disease genuinely depends on, is called ______.
options: target identification
medicinal chemistry
Expansion cohorts
MOA
questions.why: Target identification is the first step of the whole pipeline: finding the molecule the disease genuinely depends on, followed in turn by medicinal chemistry (making the compounds), preclinical (MOA and toxicology), IND-enabling studies (filing the IND), and only then the human trial phases 1A, 1B, 2 and 3. If the first step is wrong, everything after it is wasted effort; NPM1, for instance, requires the copy number data for the CNV to be read together with the mRNA expression level, and only when the two agree can it be called a driver.

questions.q: After the first step of the pipeline has identified the molecule the disease genuinely depends on, the company must still pass the two gates of disease relevance and druggability before making its final decision. In the lecturer's terminology, which step does that final decision itself correspond to?
options: Whether this molecule matters to the disease itself.
Whether this molecule can be made into a drug that hits only it and spares everything else.
The stage that turns a target into a genuinely suitable compound.
The decision the company makes about which molecule to go after.
questions.why: Target nomination is the decision the company makes about which molecule to go after, and the lecturer gives three conditions: first, the molecule must be genuinely elevated in patients' own samples, that is, it must have disease relevance; second, it must have structural tractability — a pocket in which a small molecule can sit, a surface an antibody can recognise, or a nucleic acid drug that can target it; third, the market must not be too crowded. He uses telomerase as a good example and cytoskeleton as a bad one for contrast.

questions.q: The lecturer says that MOA and toxicology are the two cornerstones of the preclinical stage. According to that explanation, which question is toxicology responsible for answering?
options: Mechanism of action — the evidence of what the compound actually does.
The study of how a compound affects a whole animal.
The complete non-clinical test package a company must work through before filing an IND with the regulator.
The whole body of development work carried out before formal human trials.
questions.why: Toxicology answers 'what does it do to a living organism', that is, the study of how a compound affects a whole animal, whereas MOA answers 'what does it do'. Only together do they form the core of IND-enabling studies: the former is the evidence of efficacy, the latter the evidence of safety, and it is the latter that is often the true determinant of the dose ceiling. The key indicators are the maximum tolerated dose and the therapeutic window; the gap between the two is the range within which patients can be treated safely.
